summary: Responses by the author of the mail protocol proposal in RFC 524 to the questions, complaints and suggestions it drew from the network community. It collects them in one place and answers each, and the author invites further discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC collects questions and suggestions about the proposed Mail Protocol and answers them. The author agrees with some changes, rejects others, and invites more comments.

sections.title: Collecting the Responses
sections.content:
James E. White says several people responded to the Mail Protocol proposal in RFC 524. RFC 555 collects their questions, complaints, and suggestions and gives the author's replies.

White says he intends to critique his own proposal in a later RFC and welcomes continued discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The author brings feedback from several readers together in one document. He plans to continue the discussion and answer further critiques.

sections.title: Verifying a Sender's Identity
sections.content:
The RFC explains that a server could ask for an ID and check it through a User Verification Function offered by another host; it says the NIC would provide such a service. Servers would not have to request proof of identity, and servers that do not require it could treat ID as a no-op.

The author distinguishes an identity check from account access and billing: an ID is intended to check authorship, while USER, PASS, and ACCT relate to access or accounting.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that wants to check who wrote a message can ask a verification service. A user ID is separate from a host password used for login or billing.

sections.title: Changes and a Minimal Server
sections.content:
White agrees with several suggestions, including changing the order of dynamic, optional, and static parameters, making the author the default signature, and warning servers about message size. He retracts his earlier position on how mail should use FTP and says a proposed unified-access approach deserves consideration.

The RFC also outlines a minimal server that can deliver mail, listing commands it must support, can treat as no-ops, or need not recognize for that function.
sections.plainLanguage: The author accepts several proposed clarifications and changes his view on FTP. He also shows a smaller command set for a server that only delivers mail.
